questions.explanation: Combining 3 and 4 gives a total of 7.
questions.misconception: Adding one extra by accident (thinking 3 + 4 = 8) is common; count the group: 3 and 4 together make exactly 7.

questions.prompt: To add 5 + 3 using counting on, you start at 5 and count forward how many more steps?
questions.explanation: Count on means begin at the first addend (5) and count forward the value of the second addend (3 steps), landing on 8.
questions.misconception: Some count from 1 instead of from the first addend — counting on should start at 5, not at 1, so the jump is only 3 steps.

questions.prompt: When adding 27 + 38 in columns, the ones column (7 + 8) sums to 15. What do you do with the 15?
options: Write 5 in the ones column and carry 1 ten to the tens column
questions.explanation: 15 is 1 ten and 5 ones: put 5 in the ones place and regroup the ten into the tens column, then 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 tens → 65.
questions.misconception: Writing all of 15 in the ones column forgets that 10 ones make a ten — the carry is what keeps the place values straight.

questions.explanation: Subtraction is the inverse of addition — 10 − 4 gets back to the 6 you started with.
questions.misconception: Multiplication is not the undo-operation for addition; only subtracting the other addend returns the original number.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true about addition order?
questions.explanation: Addition is commutative — the same two addends give the same sum in either order.
questions.misconception: Commutativity is specific to addition (and multiplication); reversing the order of the same addends never changes the total.
